newsitem.title: USA: Oil shippers promise improvements in Alaska safety.
newsitem.headline: Oil shippers promise improvements in Alaska safety.

text.p: Exxon and other oil companies will increase safety measures for oil tankers using Alaska's Prince William Sound, the site of the 1989 Exxon Valdez oil spill, Alaska Governor Tony Knowles said on Thursday.

"We will have the world's safest oil transportation system in Prince William Sound and the Gulf of Alaska," said Knowles, who returned from a trip to Texas earlier this week to convene with officials from Exxon and other companies.
"We have the commitment from those producers that that's exactly what's going to happen."
Within three months, a high-horsepower rescue tug will be stationed at Hinchinbrook Entrance, the sometimes-treacherous mouth of Prince William Sound, Knowles said at a news conference.

That 11,200-horsepower tug will reduce risks of drift groundings in a "very perilous part of the route" that oil tankers take from the Valdez marine terminal of the trans-Alaska pipeline, Knowles said.

Shippers later this month will also test a new tractor tug, a vessel much more manoeuvrable than the conventional tugs that escort oil-laden tankers through Prince William Sound, the Democratic governor said.
If the test shows that the tractor tug is as good as or better than the conventional tugs, "we have the commitment that that's the tug we're going to have," he said.
If the tests show problems with the tractor tug, the shippers have agreed to build a state-of-the-art vessel to fit Alaska conditions, Knowles said.
The tug agreement is with the seven oil companies that own the Alyeska Pipeline Service Co, the consortium that operates the trans-Alaska oil pipeline.
British Petroleum, Atlantic Richfield Co (Arco) and Exxon together own about 90 percent of Alyeska and dominate oil shipping in Prince William Sound.
The cost of the escort tug upgrades will be borne by the shippers and the state, said Alaska Natural Resources Commissioner John Shively.
The escort system was mandated by state and federal laws passed after the grounding of the Exxon Valdez tanker, which spilled 11 million gallons of oil.
In Texas, Knowles met with officials from Anadarko Petroleum, Union Texas Petroleum and Marathon as well as Exxon.
Anadarko and Union Texas have vastly increased their Alaska activities in recent years.

The companies are partners with Arco in the new Alpine field west of the North Slope's Kuparuk River unit. Alpine is estimated to hold 250 million to 300 million barrels of recoverable light crude oil and production is expected to start in 2000.

Anadarko and Union Texas are among the smaller oil companies that missed out on the original North Slope boom but are enthusiastic about new opportunties in Alaska, said Alaska Commerce Commissioner Willie Hensley.
"They're not just riding on the coat-tails of the majors. They have (new) ideas," Hensley said.
